newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-DOPING MUTES RUSSIA'S CELEBRATIONS.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-DOPING MUTES RUSSIA'S CELEBRATIONS.

text.p: Russia, in a state of shock after Lyubov Yegorova's disqualification for doping, were not in the mood to celebrate after winning the women's relay gold at the Nordic skiing world championships on Thursday.
"It was a big shock and it was hard to find some sleep but we are top athletes and we did our best to win," said Yelena Vialbe, who completed the last lap for the Russian team.

A few hours earlier, Yegorova, who was stripped of her gold medal in Sunday's five-km race on Wednesday for testing positive for the banned stimulant Bromantan, had left the Trondheim championships discretely by car, witnesses said.
Before the start of the race, Vialbe took a microphone and addressed the crowd saying the Russian team felt sorry but not responsible.

"The whole team wants to apologise to the public and the king (King Harald of Norway) for what happened but you must understand that Lyubov Yegorova acted individually and that the team is not to blame," she said.

The International Ski Federation (FIS) general secretary Gian Franco Kasper said on Wednesday that Yegorova had admitted taking a Bromantan pill. She said she had taken it not knowing it was banned and was the only one responsible for doing it, Kasper added.
Yegorova told Russia's Sport Express newspaper she had reached "automatically" for an old pack of Bromantan she had had since she won three golds at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics.

"I didn't understand the substance was banned," she said. "You'd have to be suicidal to take Bromantan knowing it was banned. Believe me, I really didn't know. It's a nightmare to get caught for such a trifle."

The 30-year-old Yegorova's admission was a big embarrassment for Russian sport so soon after controversy over the use of the same substance, a stimulant-cum-masking agent, by some Russian athletes at last year's Atlanta Olympics.
Yegorova, who won six Olympic titles and three world titles before coming to Trondheim, had been fighting to recapture her best form since her brilliant showing in Lillehammer.

After the Games she retired temporarily from competition to give birth to a son, Viktor, and then experienced health problems. Her best result this season before the world championships was a third place in a World Cup race last month in Kavgolovo, Russia.
Alexander Grishun, head coach of the Russian women's team, said on Thursday Yegorova was finished in the sport and had no chance of being picked for next year's Nagano Olympics.
"I fear that she'll have to accept she is finished with the Olympics and with skiing in general," he said.
There have been continuing allegations of doping in Nordic skiing in the last few months and FIS introduced new, pre-race blood tests at this year's world championships.
The tests are aimed at detecting blood doping which allows the blood to transport more oxygen to the working muscles.
Medical sources said Yegorova's case had nothing to do with blood doping. Bromantan was traced in urine taken from her at a routine, post-race test.
A second test on another sample was not needed as she admitted wrongdoing, Kasper said.
Norway's Trude Dybendahl-Hartz, a member of the Norwegian team who came second in the relay, congratulated FIS for taking swift action.

"It's comforting to see that FIS are capable of finding those who cheat and of punishing them straight away," she said. "I'm very sad for my sport. I'm not naive and I knew there was some doping going on. I feel sorry for Russia but I'm pleased to see that the system put in place by FIS works."
